title: Format a hex view
description:
Write `hexView(address, bytes, readable)`. `bytes` and `readable` have the same length; `readable[i]` says whether `bytes[i]` was actually read. Produce one line per 16 bytes, starting at `address` (which you may assume is a multiple of 16):

- the row's address as 16 upper-case hex digits, then two spaces;
- 16 byte columns, each two upper-case hex digits (or `??` if unreadable) followed by one space, with one **extra** space after the eighth; for a short last row, pad the missing bytes with three spaces each (and the extra space if the gap includes the middle);
- then two more spaces (in addition to the last column's trailing space) and the text: each readable byte from 0x20 to 0x7E as itself, anything else (including unreadable bytes) as `.`. Missing bytes on a short last row add nothing to the text.

Lines end with `\n`. For no bytes, return an empty string.

```
hexView(0x1000, "Rook" + 12 zero bytes + 0x0E, all readable except the last) =
"0000000000001000  52 6F 6F 6B 00 00 00 00  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00   Rook............\n"
"0000000000001010  ??                                                 .\n"
```
hints: Build each row in two parts at once: the hex columns into the output, and the text column into a separate string, appended at the end of the row after two spaces.
Add the extra space after the eighth column (`i == 7`) whether or not that column held a byte, so short rows still line up.
`std::format("{:016X}", n)` gives 16 upper-case hex digits; `{:02X}` gives two.
